summary: The developer machine has the core tools and DocumentDB skills needed to build the Node.js LangChain orchestration sample and to verify it against the live Azure DocumentDB cluster. The DocumentDB data-plane MCP server and a rich set of DocumentDB skills are installed and were used to ground and correct several cold answers that described older Cosmos DB behaviors (resource types, connection endpoints, billing model, and search/index commands). Missing items are accelerators (DocumentDB Agent Kit) and some non-blocking developer tools (mongosh); a few implementation decisions required by the prompt (LLM provider, news source, webhook schema, embedding model/dimension) remain unspecified and must be chosen by the builder.
summary_points: Ready to start: Node.js, npm/npx, az, docker, the documentdb MCP server (data-plane), and 16 DocumentDB skills are installed and available for development and verification.

Several cold answers were outdated or confused with the older Cosmos DB (RU) model or other products — the correct resources use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters, az documentdb CLI commands, vCore/compute-tier billing, new connection-host suffixes, built-in $search and cosmosSearch vector indexes, and Microsoft Entra ID data-plane auth.
Missing accelerators: DocumentDB Agent Kit is not installed and would speed sample scaffolding (install via: npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit).
Local developer tooling: a supported local DocumentDB Gateway Docker image exists (port 10260); mongosh is not on PATH but is optional because the documentdb MCP server provides inspection tooling.
Open implementation choices (LLM provider, news source, webhook auth, embedding model/dimension) are information gaps that the builder must decide before coding the sample.

tools.name: node / npm / npx
tools.needed_for: Run and build the Node.js LangChain orchestration sample, install packages, run npm scripts and npx for MCP skill tooling.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run or bootstrap the sample, install skills, or run the demo.
tools.workaround: Install Node.js 24+; for one-off checks use a different machine with Node installed.

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Inspect Azure resources, manage firewall or networking during verification, optionally retrieve cluster metadata if permissioned.
tools.impact_if_missing: Would lose easy control-plane checks and firewall-rule management; some verification steps (like retrieving ARM-managed connection metadata) would be harder.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server for data-plane verification; ask infra owner to provide connection metadata or run az for you.

references.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Run local DocumentDB Gateway container for local integration testing (port 10260).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run a local DocumentDB gateway container for offline integration tests; must test against the live cluster.
tools.workaround: Run tests against the live cluster (skill_md says a live cluster exists) or obtain another machine with Docker.

tools.name: documentdb MCP server
tools.needed_for: Data-plane inspection, listing databases/collections, creating indexes, running explain(), inserting sample documents and verifying what the app created.
tools.detail: documentdb MCP server with 18 data-plane tools (list_databases, find_documents, create_index, explain_operation, insert_documents, etc.). Use connection_profile "default" for this cluster.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder for an agent to run safe read-only queries, list indexes, or run explain plans; builder would need mongosh or interactive portal access.
tools.workaround: Use mongosh (if available) or the Azure Portal; but documentdb MCP is the preferred programmatic inspection route.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Authoritative Microsoft documentation search and fetch to ground cold answers and to find exact CLI/ARM/Bicep examples.
tools.detail: learn_microsoft_docs_search and fetch tools are available.
tools.impact_if_missing: Agent would have to rely on web search or local memory; risk of using outdated or incorrect guidance.
tools.workaround: Use web search externally and paste results into the build environment; request the missing docs be added to MCP.

tools.name: Installed DocumentDB skills (documentdb-azure-deployment, documentdb-connection, documentdb-driver, documentdb-data-modeling, documentdb-indexing, documentdb-local-deployment, documentdb-vector-search, documentdb-full-text-search, documentdb-security, documentdb-monitoring, documentdb-query-optimizer, documentdb-natural-language-querying, documentdb-high-availability, documentdb-storage, documentdb-sharding)
tools.needed_for: Authoritative, scenario-specific guidance on deployment, connection tuning, driver patterns, indexing, vector search, full-text search, local dev, security, HA, monitoring and schema decisions.
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder would lack curated, product-specific best practices and code examples for DocumentDB; they might use general MongoDB advice that is incorrect for this managed service.
tools.workaround: Rely on Microsoft Learn pages and general MongoDB guidance; install the DocumentDB Agent Kit (accelerator) to restore parity.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Ad-hoc connectivity checks, manual shell-based index inspection and query testing.
tools.impact_if_missing: Manual CLI-based checks are harder; however the documentdb MCP server can run queries and explain plans programmatically.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server's find / explain / list index tools, or install mongosh locally (`npm i -g @mongosh/cli` / download), or use MongoDB Compass with the provided connection string.

references.title: Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB

tools.name: azd / bicep / terraform / dotnet
tools.needed_for: Infrastructure-as-code provisioning (Bicep / Terraform / azd) or .NET sample code runtime (dotnet).
tools.detail: azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet not found on PATH (per inventory).
tools.impact_if_missing: These are optional for this sample (run-environment forbids provisioning a new cluster); if the builder wanted to include IaC or .NET examples they would need to add these tools.
tools.workaround: Skip infra provisioning (use existing cluster as required by skill_md); use Node.js-only sample as requested.

tools.name: az login (Azure sign-in credential)
tools.needed_for: Any control-plane checks or firewall rule adjustments during verification.
tools.detail: Signed in: Visual Studio Enterprise subscription present in the az session.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run az-based control-plane checks or retrieve ARM-managed metadata.
tools.workaround: Ask an operator with az access to run the control-plane steps; use the documentdb MCP server for data-plane verification.

accelerators_missed: DocumentDB Agent Kit (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit)

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (resource type string used in ARM/Bicep).
confusions.grounded_answer: The current managed Azure DocumentDB cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (API 2025-09-01). Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts refers to Azure Cosmos DB account resources (legacy naming) and is not the primary resource type for the new DocumentDB managed clusters.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB examples and the historical 'DatabaseAccount' resource type (Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) have similar names; the cold answer described the older Cosmos DB account resource rather than the new mongoClusters resource.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts in ARM/Bicep for this sample, deployment instructions and CLI commands would target the wrong resource type and any IaC templates or CLI snippets generated would be invalid for DocumentDB clusters.
improvements: Add a prominent note to the top of the Azure DocumentDB quickstarts and the documentdb MCP skill that the managed cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.
Update any agent-kit skill or code-generation templates to prefer mongoClusters for DocumentDB cluster creation.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Examples: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB; az cosmosdb update ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the az documentdb command group (extension) and its mongocluster subcommands (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create / show / list / reset-password). A documentdb az extension may be installed on first use or via az extension add --name documentdb.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI
az documentdb mongocluster create (az CLI reference)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Azure Cosmos DB's older MongoDB-compatible accounts use az cosmosdb; the new DocumentDB managed cluster is surfaced under az documentdb (CLI extension) so the command group differs.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands or relying on the cosmosdb command group would call the wrong control-plane APIs and fail or operate on a different account type.
improvements: Document the required az extension (documentdb) and show the exact az documentdb mongocluster commands in the agent kit README and the quickstart landing page.
Add a brief migration note: 'If you previously used az cosmosdb for Cosmos DB accounts, use az documentdb for DocumentDB clusters.'

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts ... Terraform azurerm_cosmosdb_account ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/ARM and Terraform deploy the DocumentDB managed cluster using Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep) or azurerm_mongo_cluster (Terraform AzureRM provider) which target the mongoClusters API (2025-09-01). The older Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts and azurerm_cosmosdb_account target Cosmos DB account resources.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' / azurerm_cosmosdb_account resources historically represented MongoDB-compatible Cosmos DB accounts; the new DocumentDB product uses a different top-level resource (mongoClusters).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder generated Bicep/Terraform using databaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account, the templates will not be correct for DocumentDB clusters and will fail to provision or address the wrong resource.
improvements: Update Bicep and Terraform quickstarts in docs and the agent skills to use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and azurerm_mongo_cluster examples.
Add a deprecation warning on pages that still use databaseAccounts for MongoDB-like clusters.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Standard MongoDB URI example: mongodb://<user>:<pass>@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false... Host suffix: .mongo.cosmos.azure.com. Port 10255 TLS.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB clusters use mongodb+srv URIs that target the cluster's mongocluster host like <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com (SRV form) or mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000. The older .mongo.cosmos.azure.com + port 10255 pattern describes classic Cosmos DB MongoDB API endpoints, not the new DocumentDB cluster hostnames.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB MongoDB API docs and examples use hostnames like *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and port 10255; the new managed DocumentDB clusters use different host suffixes and SRV patterns (global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com).

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix or port will fail connections or connect to a different service; missing required options (tls=true, retryWrites=false) will cause connection failures or unexpected driver behavior.
improvements: Add a small 'Connection string differences' note on the top of both DocumentDB and Cosmos DB MongoDB quickstarts showing the correct SRV host suffix for DocumentDB clusters and the legacy Cosmos host/port for older accounts.
In the documentdb MCP skill, include a one-line copyable example for Node.js showing the recommended connection URI and driver options (tls=true, retryWrites=false, authMechanism if using OIDC).

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary billing model is Request Units (RU/s) — provisioned throughput at the account or container level ... There is also a serverless option ... Additionally, Azure offers newer dedicated vCore based clusters for the MongoDB API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the managed DocumentDB clusters) uses compute tiers (vCore-style compute tiers such as M10..M200) and storage pricing (compute + storage billing), not the RU/s model. RU-based throughput describes Azure Cosmos DB's classic RU model; DocumentDB cluster pricing is compute/storage (vCores) oriented with optional free tier clusters.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The RU billing model is the classic Cosmos DB model; some MongoDB-compatible offerings on Azure (Cosmos DB for MongoDB) historically used RU throughput. Azure DocumentDB is a vCore/compute-tier product and the two models are often conflated.

confusion_sources.title: Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas

confusions.build_risk: If the builder expects RU/s scaling and autoscale APIs, they might design indexing and micro-benchmarking around RU consumption and use control-plane APIs that don't exist for DocumentDB clusters.
improvements: Add a clear pricing comparison table in the quickstart landing page: 'DocumentDB clusters (vCore tiers M10..M200) vs Cosmos DB RU model', highlighting the correct billing model.
Add a note in the agent-kit about which pricing model applies to each product to avoid the RU vs vCore confusion.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB API the normal data-plane authentication method is MongoDB SCRAM (username/password) — AAD data-plane authentication is not supported for the MongoDB API; drivers should authenticate with SCRAM credentials.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native (SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC / MONGODB-OIDC) data-plane authentication. Drivers can authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID by using an OIDC-based connection string (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC/ MONGODB-OIDC or MONGODB-OIDC+env/TOKEN_RESOURCE properties) or by using a managed identity scenario (registering the managed identity and using a client id in the SRV URI). See the 'how-to-connect-role-based-access-control' docs for examples and required connection-string properties.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically some MongoDB-compatible offerings required only SCRAM credentials; documentation and community posts that pre-date Entra ID support cause agents to assume AAD isn't supported for data-plane auth.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes AAD is unsupported, they may choose to store long-lived SCRAM credentials inappropriately or miss an opportunity to use managed identities for secure auth.
improvements: Add a short 'data-plane auth options' table to the quickstart and connection guidance showing examples for SCRAM and Microsoft Entra ID (including sample SRV URIs and required authMechanismProperties).
Add a sample Node.js snippet in the documentdb-driver skill showing how to connect using Microsoft Entra ID (or refer to the how-to-connect role-based doc).

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the official MongoDB drivers for the language (for Node.js use the mongodb npm package). Do not use the Azure Cosmos DB SQL API SDK for MongoDB API workloads — use the standard MongoDB client.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the official MongoDB drivers (Node.js: mongodb package) because DocumentDB speaks the MongoDB wire protocol. There is no distinct 'DocumentDB-for-MongoDB' service-specific runtime SDK for application code; use MongoDB drivers and apply DocumentDB driver tuning (retryWrites=false, TLS, pool sizing) from documentdb-driver and documentdb-connection skills.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None if the official MongoDB drivers are used with the recommended options.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Vector-capable clusters expose vector index types such as HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. Index creation is done via a MongoDB createIndex call on the embedding field with engine-specific options (e.g., { embedding: 'vector' }, { engine: 'hnsw', engineParams: {...}, dimensions: 1536 }).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector indexes under the native 'cosmosSearch' vector index family with subtypes such as vector-diskann, vector-hnsw, and vector-ivf. Indexes are created through the service's createSearchIndexes / index-creation commands (documentdb-vector-search skill) and queried through the $search / cosmosSearch aggregation stage. The exact options and the command form are DocumentDB-specific (not necessarily identical to createIndex engine:'hnsw' syntax used in some platforms).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a MongoDB/Atlas-style createIndex syntax; DocumentDB exposes vector indexing via its cosmosSearch vector index family and uses service-specific index creation commands/definitions.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder issues the wrong createIndex call, the cluster will reject it; the builder might create an incorrect index format or fail to create an index at all.
improvements: Add a concrete, copy-pasteable example for creating a vector index (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF) in the documentdb-vector-search skill and on the quickstart page.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no built-in rich Atlas-Search equivalent in Cosmos DB's MongoDB API; use Azure Cognitive Search integrated with Cosmos DB or an external search service.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB includes built-in full-text search (via createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage) and native hybrid search capability (BM25 lexical search via $search plus vector retrieval via cosmosSearch) enabling combined BM25 + vector retrieval workflows without an external search service.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB articles and community posts often recommended Azure Cognitive Search for rich text search on Cosmos DB; DocumentDB's newer search primitives (createSearchIndexes + $search) are newer and less widely referenced in older materials.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes no native full-text search, they may architect an external search service, increasing complexity and cost unnecessarily.
improvements: Place a 'search capabilities' note on the quickstart landing page showing $search examples and how to combine BM25 with vector search (RRF).
Include a small example in the sample repo that uses createSearchIndexes + $search to demonstrate BM25 + vector hybrid retrieval.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API exposes server versions; modern clusters support recent wire versions (4.0, 4.2, 5.0 and newer — some clusters now support MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol). Some features differ or are missing (mapReduce, admin commands).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 and provides ~99.03% operator compatibility. Some administrative commands and a small subset of aggregation stages/operators differ or are not exposed; always verify feature compatibility with the compatibility docs before relying on advanced features.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer gave a mixture of older MongoDB version examples and hedged wording; the official docs enumerate supported wire protocol versions explicitly (5.0–8.0).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes a different wire-version set they might pick incompatible driver features or rely on unsupported server features.
improvements: Make the supported wire protocol versions (5.0–8.0) clearly visible on the quickstart and compatibility pages and add a short 'which server version to pick' note for clusters.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no fully equivalent local emulator; the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator primarily targets the SQL API and has limited MongoDB API support on Windows. Use a local MongoDB server (mongodb:latest) for unit-level development. When connecting to the live cluster use port 10255 (TLS).
confusions.grounded_answer: There is a supported local DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) that exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 for local development; connect with TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256 (and use the documentdb-local-deployment guidance). The older Cosmos DB emulator comment is not the correct path for DocumentDB local testing.

grounding_links.title: Local Developer Gateway image (Gateway on port 10260)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Community memory about Cosmos DB emulator and cross-product naming led to assuming no local image exists; DocumentDB provides a local gateway image, but it's newer and less widely cited in older posts.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes no local gateway, they may run integration tests against the live cluster unnecessarily, incurring cost and adding risk.
improvements: Add a short 'local dev' section in the quickstart referencing the Gateway Docker image and a minimal docker-compose snippet to encourage local integration testing.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB exposes a change feed and the MongoDB API may expose change-stream-like behavior depending on the MongoDB wire version your account supports. If the MongoDB API supports change streams for your account's server version you can use driver watch(); otherwise use the Cosmos DB change feed. Some accounts may require enabling the appropriate API/version or feature flag at provisioning time.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams (including multishard change streams); they are available via the standard MongoDB change stream APIs (watch(), $changeStream) and some multi-shard features (multi-shard change streams) must be enabled in the cluster features page. Pre-images and historical replay features are controllable via collection/cluster features and the docs describe how to enable them.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a — the cold answer was hedged but fundamentally correct that support depends on server version and feature enablement.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder doesn't enable multi-shard change streams when needed they won't be able to watch across shards; the docs provide the enablement steps.
improvements: Add a short checklist in the local sample README describing when and how to enable change streams for the cluster (and when pre-images are required).

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server profile for data-plane inspection and tools tailored to Cosmos DB / DocumentDB. The general azure MCP server covers ARM/management plane but the documentdb MCP server provides document/collection inspection, index and query-plan tools specific to Cosmos DB / MongoDB API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server is the data-plane toolset (it is installed and exposes the needed collection-level tools). The azure MCP server covers control-plane/ARM and best-practice lookups but not data-plane query/index inspection.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None — documentdb MCP is present in the inventory and is the correct tool for data-plane tasks.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: The original managed document database from Microsoft was called DocumentDB; it evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (multi-model). Azure Cosmos DB is the current service; the old DocumentDB name lives on historically. This Microsoft DocumentDB/CosmosDB is not the same as any unrelated open-source project named "DocumentDB" — Cosmos DB is a proprietary Microsoft service implementing multiple APIs (SQL, MongoDB, Gremlin, Table, Cassandra).
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly incorrect / ambiguous: 'DocumentDB' historically referred to the earlier Azure DocumentDB (the pre-Cosmos DB offering). The new managed service named 'Azure DocumentDB' is a recent vCore-based product distinct from 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU)' and from the open-source DocumentDB engine (the engine project exists and is related). The naming is a source of confusion: some older docs use 'vCore-based Cosmos DB for MongoDB' and the new first-party 'Azure DocumentDB' name reclaims the DocumentDB brand. The relationship: Azure DocumentDB is a Microsoft-managed service built on the open-source DocumentDB engine — it is not the old Cosmos DB account resource.

grounding_links.title: Moving from another MongoDB-compatible service to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Product naming has changed over time and the 'DocumentDB' name was used historically by Microsoft and also exists as an open-source engine project; older references conflate Cosmos DB, legacy DocumentDB, and newly branded DocumentDB clusters.

confusion_sources.title: Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas

confusions.build_risk: Confusing product names could lead builders to use wrong docs (Cosmos DB pages) or wrong control-plane APIs, causing IaC or CLI errors.
improvements: Add a short 'Naming history' blurb on the quickstart landing page that clearly states: 'Azure DocumentDB (managed mongoClusters) — not the Cosmos DB databaseAccount resource; not Amazon DocumentDB; engine: open-source DocumentDB.'

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the MongoDB API the backend is Cosmos DB's storage engine (not an actual mongod process). Because of that apps should use MongoDB drivers but be aware of semantic differences.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB the managed service is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the microsoft/documentdb project) rather than being a thin Cosmos DB layer. Nevertheless, the surface is MongoDB wire-compatibility and apps should use MongoDB drivers; there are platform-level semantic differences (admin commands, some aggregation stages, index behavior) documented in the compatibility docs.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Community and older product messaging often lumped Cosmos DB's MongoDB compatibility and other Azure MongoDB-like offerings together; the new DocumentDB service is a distinct engine implementation and product.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes the Cosmos DB engine semantics, they might mis-handle features like indexing or admin commands; but using MongoDB drivers and testing against the actual cluster mitigates risk.
improvements: Add a short 'engine & compatibility' note in the quickstart that clarifies: 'Engine: DocumentDB (open-source). API: MongoDB wire protocol. Compatibility: 99.03% of MongoDB operators — see compatibility page.'

confusions.question: What database and collection names will the sample use and where is the connection string read from?
confusions.cold_answer: Database: sample_fintech_11. Collection for articles: articles (store scored articles). Collection for watchlist: watchlist. Read connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime; do not store secrets in files.
confusions.grounded_answer: Database name 'sample_fintech_11' is specified by the run-environment and must be used. Collection naming (articles, watchlist) is an implementation choice for the sample and is not enforced by the platform; connection string location (DOCUMENTDB_URI env var) is correct per skill_md and run guidance.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The database name was specified in the prompt run-environment; collection names were a builder choice in the cold answer rather than a required item.
confusions.build_risk: Minor: builder must ensure they use exactly 'sample_fintech_11' for DB operations; collection names can be chosen, but must be consistently used in verification steps via the documentdb MCP server.
improvements: Add a brief sample-convention line in the run-environment docs suggesting a canonical collection name (e.g., sentiment_signals) so sample authors converge on the same names for verification tooling.

confusions.question: What Node.js client and exact connect command will the sample use to open a connection?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the official mongodb driver (npm install mongodb). Example connect code: const { MongoClient } = require('mongodb'); const client = new MongoClient(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true }); await client.connect(); const db = client.db('sample_fintech_11');
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the official mongodb driver and the singleton MongoClient pattern. Additionally, DocumentDB recommends driver options and connection-string flags such as tls=true, retryWrites=false and driver tuning via the documentdb-driver and documentdb-connection guidance; the exact options vary by driver major version (Node.js driver 5/6/7).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a generic MongoClient code sample without DocumentDB-specific recommended connection options (retryWrites=false, tls=true and possibly authMechanism adjustments).
confusions.build_risk: Minor runtime issues: missing retryWrites=false may cause errors, or missing TLS flags may be rejected. Following documentdb-driver and documentdb-connection guidance avoids these pitfalls.
improvements: Add a short Node.js example in the documentdb-driver skill showing the recommended options for MongoClient when connecting to DocumentDB (including recommended driver versions and retryWrites=false).

confusions.question: What index definition will the sample create for embeddings (vector search)?
confusions.cold_answer: Create an embedding vector index on the articles collection with an HNSW index. Example (approximate): await db.collection('articles').createIndex( { embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_hnsw', engine: 'hnsw', engineParams: { m: 16, efConstruction: 200 }, similarity: 'cosine', dimensions: 1536 } );
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB uses the cosmosSearch vector index family (vector-diskann, vector-hnsw, vector-ivf). Index creation is done through the service's createSearchIndexes/createSearchIndexes-like commands and index definition format documented in the vector-search skill; the exact createIndex engine:... syntax used by Atlas is not guaranteed to work and must be constructed per the DocumentDB index-definition schema.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer proposed an Atlas-style createIndex signature; DocumentDB uses a different index-creation facility (cosmosSearch) and the exact field names/options may differ.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder issues Atlas-style createIndex commands they will be rejected; the builder must use the documentdb MCP server or the vector skill examples to create a compatible index.
improvements: Provide a minimal concrete example (copy-paste) of createSearchIndexes for a vector index in the vector-search skill and documentation so sample authors don't invent Atlas-style syntaxes.

confusions.question: How will the sample store and query scored articles for the orchestration pipeline?
confusions.cold_answer: Each scored article document will be inserted into sample_fintech_11.articles with fields: { _id, headline, url, publishedAt, text, score: <sentiment score>, tickers: [ 'AAPL', ... ], embedding: <float32 array> }. Query for alerts by finding documents where tickers overlap a watchlist entry and score passes threshold: db.articles.find({ tickers: { $in: ['AAPL'] }, score: { $lte: -0.5 } }). For vector nearest-neighbour searches use a vector search command against the embedding index.
confusions.grounded_answer: The proposed schema is reasonable. DocumentDB-specific advice: create a multikey index on tickers, an index on timestamp, and use createSearchIndexes + cosmosSearch for vector and hybrid retrieval as needed. The collection name is implementation choice; be consistent with verification scripts that use the documentdb MCP server.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed a plausible implementation schema with Atlas-like vector commands; schema proposal is fine but vector/index creation must follow DocumentDB commands.
confusions.build_risk: Minor: ensure indexes exist for the watchlist queries (tickers multikey and timestamp); otherwise the alert queries may be slow or cause COLLSCANs.
improvements: Add a cookbook example in the data-modeling skill that shows the 'sentiment_signals' schema, the recommended indexes (tickers multikey, timestamp, search index), and sample queries used by the sample.

confusions.question: Which operations will the sample use the documentdb MCP server for during development?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (profile 'default') to inspect collections and indexes, validate the created vector index and view query plans; use it to run explain() for expensive queries and to confirm that the articles collection and indexes were created successfully.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server is available and appropriate for these data-plane verification tasks (list DBs, sample documents, create/list indexes, explain operations).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None; the MCP server provides these capabilities and is present in the inventory.

information_gaps.title: LLM provider and credentials
information_gaps.description: The prompt requires a sentiment/ticker-extraction agent but neither the starter prompt nor any skill declares which LLM provider to use (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, local model) or where its API key lives; I looked in the prompt_review, skill_md and installed skills but found no specification. The builder must choose a provider and add the related env var (e.g., OPENAI_API_KEY or AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT + AZURE_OPENAI_KEY) and document it in .env.example.

information_gaps.title: News source for the scraper
information_gaps.description: No authoritative recommendation for which news source (public RSS feeds, NewsAPI, paid feed) to use is present in the prompt or skills; the builder must pick feeds or require an API key. I searched the prompt_review and skill_md and found no guidance.

information_gaps.title: Notification / webhook schema and authentication
information_gaps.description: The prompt asks to 'fire notifications' but does not define JSON payload shape, expected headers, or auth method. The builder must choose a secure webhook schema (HMAC signature, bearer token, or managed identity) and document it; this information is not in any skill or docs.

information_gaps.title: Embedding model and vector dimension
information_gaps.description: If the sample will create vector indexes and embeddings, the embedding model and its output dimension (e.g., OpenAI embedding dims or a local model) must be chosen to match vector index 'dimensions'. No skill or prompt specifies which model to use; I inspected documentdb-vector-search but it assumes the builder picks a model and dimensions.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters as the ARM/Bicep resource type for DocumentDB clusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).
Use az documentdb mongocluster ... CLI commands (install the 'documentdb' az extension if needed) for cluster management rather than az cosmosdb.

sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Read the DocumentDB connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI and ensure it includes TLS and retryWrites=false (use SRV form if provided) before passing to MongoClient; follow documentdb-driver and documentdb-connection guidance for recommended MongoClient options.

If you will use vector search, create vector indexes using the DocumentDB cosmosSearch index facilities (documentdb-vector-search) and verify index creation with the documentdb MCP server instead of using Atlas-style createIndex signatures.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample (the run-environment uses an existing cluster and azd is optional for deployments). Do not install unless you intend to add IaC provisioning to the sample.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for the code sample as the cluster is pre-provisioned; add only if you plan to include a local IaC deploy path in the repo. If not present, the documentdb-azure-deployment skill's templates can be referenced instead.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for the sample run. Add only if you intend to include Terraform-based provisioning examples; otherwise rely on the existing cluster and the documentdb-azure-deployment skill's templates.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this Node.js sample. Install only if you need to run .NET-based repo examples or tests.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Worth adding for interactive manual checks (index inspection, quick queries) during development. Install mongosh on PATH (npm i -g @mongosh/cli) or use MongoDB Compass with the documented SRV connection string as a GUI alternative. If not installed, rely on the documentdb MCP server's data-plane tools for scripted checks.
